books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

primary_sources: Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, August 1810
Henry Clay, Speech on the Increase of the Navy, January 22, 1812
James Monroe, seventh annual message to Congress, December 2, 1823

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note); Tecumseh, Clay, and Monroe excerpts verified against Wikisource and the Avalon Project
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the United States expanded its power and territory on the world stage in the period 1800-1848.

documents.title: The Louisiana Purchase
documents.source: Treaty between the United States and France, April 30, 1803, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The treaty France and the United States signed after Napoleon offered the whole Louisiana Territory.
documents.text: France ceded the Louisiana Territory to the United States for $15 million. The land stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains and from the Gulf of Mexico to Canada, and it included New Orleans, the port at the mouth of the Mississippi. The purchase nearly doubled the size of the United States in a single treaty.

documents.title: Tecumseh warns Harrison
documents.source: Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, Vincennes, August 1810, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Tecumseh, a Shawnee leader, speaking to the governor of the Indiana Territory about land sales.
documents.text: “Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawanoes, the Winnebagos, the Delawares and the Miamis, and have taken our lands. . . . The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land, as it was at first, and should be yet, for it was never divided, but belongs to all.”

documents.title: Henry Clay urges war
documents.source: Henry Clay, Speech on the Increase of the Navy, House of Representatives, January 22, 1812, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Clay, a leader of the War Hawks, urging Congress to build a navy five months before war was declared.
documents.text: “Sir, if you wish to avoid foreign commerce; give up all your prosperity. It is the thing protected, not the instrument of protection, that involves you in war. Commerce engenders collision, collision war, and war, the argument supposes, leads to despotism. . . . No, sir.”

documents.title: The Treaty of Ghent
documents.source: Treaty of Ghent, December 24, 1814, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The peace treaty that ended the War of 1812, signed in Belgium after two and a half years of war.
documents.text: The treaty ended the war where it had begun. Both sides agreed to stop fighting, to give back any territory seized during the war, and to recognize the boundary between the United States and Canada that had been fixed before the war. The treaty said nothing about the American grievances that had caused the war: aid to Native peoples, interference with American shipping, or the impressment of American sailors.

documents.title: The Hartford Convention
documents.source: Report of the Hartford Convention, January 1815, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Federalist delegates from New England, meeting in Hartford, Connecticut, to protest the war.
documents.text: In December 1814, as diplomats negotiated an end to the War of 1812, Federalist delegates from New England met at Hartford to protest the war and the power of the Democratic-Republican government. A few radical delegates talked of New England leaving the Union, but the convention rejected secession. It proposed amendments to the Constitution, including a two-thirds vote of Congress to declare war, and sent delegates to Washington, arriving just as news came that the war had ended.

documents.title: The Adams-Onís Treaty
documents.sourcing: The treaty negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams, transferring Florida from Spain.
documents.text: Spain gave Florida to the United States, and the United States gave up any claim to Texas. The two nations also fixed the boundary between the Louisiana Territory and Spanish land to the west. Florida had become a concern because enslaved people escaping from Georgia found refuge there, and because General Andrew Jackson had invaded Florida during the First Seminole War.

documents.title: The Treaty of Wanghia
documents.source: Treaty of Wanghia, 1844, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The treaty the United States signed with China after Britain won trading privileges there.
documents.text: In the Treaty of Wanghia, China extended to the United States the same trading privileges it had extended to Great Britain. American merchants could trade at Chinese ports on the same terms as the British, ending the unofficial Old China Trade that had run since the Revolution. The treaty carried American commerce into Asia on terms set by a European power's earlier bargain.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the United States expanded its power and territory on the world stage, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of expansion does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Napoleonic Wars disrupting American trade, the Louisiana Purchase opening the West, or the new Latin American republics winning independence.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument, such as the Louisiana Purchase, Clay's speech, or the Monroe Doctrine.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents that show the limits of expansion.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Barbary Wars, the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842, or the Oregon settlement of 1846.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Tecumseh speaking to the governor who bought the land, or Clay urging war before it was declared.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where the United States expanded and where it did not, or weighing territorial gains against the limits of American power.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The United States expanded its territory enormously between 1800 and 1848, nearly doubling in 1803 and adding Florida and a Pacific claim, but its power on the world stage grew more slowly: it could buy land and warn Europe, but it could not win a war outright or enforce its own warnings.
Context: The Napoleonic Wars left American trade at the mercy of Britain and France, and the new republic's army and navy were small. Napoleon needed cash for war in Europe and had lost Haiti, which is why he sold Louisiana at all.
Evidence of expansion: Document 1 gives the Louisiana Purchase, $15 million for land to the Rockies; Document 6 gives Florida from Spain in 1819; Document 7 shows American trade reaching China on British terms by 1844.
Evidence of limits: Document 2 has Tecumseh resisting the land sales that expansion depended on; Document 3 shows Clay urging war because peaceful pressure had failed; Document 4 has the Treaty of Ghent ending the war with no territory gained and no grievance answered; Document 5 shows New England Federalists protesting the war itself.
Beyond the documents: The Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warned Europe out of the Americas, but the British navy enforced it; the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 and the Oregon compromise of 1846 settled borders by bargain, not by force.
Complexity: Expansion was real but uneven: the United States bought and bargained its way to a continental size, while its power abroad rested on other nations' navies and on the weakness of Spain and France, not on its own strength.
